extracted.intended_audience: aspiring and practicing fiction writers; students of creative writing; critics interested in craft
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and aesthetic guidance for composing fiction—both short stories and novels—covering selection, subject, form, style, characterization, narrative technique, and moral/psychological aim. Emphasizes matching subject to talent, disciplined style, and the selective transposition of life into art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need of selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Any theory of fiction must begin by assuming the need of selection; choose between material and omit remotely relevant or irrelevant facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection is the first step toward coherent expression: a narrative cannot include every accidental propinquity in time or space. The novelist must choose what to keep and what to discard to produce a coherent work; failure to select leads to formlessness or the 'slice of life' trap. (Anti-pattern: packing the tale with irrelevant factual debris.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Form as order; style as presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Form is the order, in time and importance, in which incidents are grouped; style is the way they are presented — the medium of the narrator's mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form and style should spring naturally from the chosen theme. Style is a discipline: habit makes the style of the writer. Aim for precision of words and a medium that 'gives back' the incidents with the proper quality. (Example: Proust's 'severity of taste' and refusal to write anything not 'c'est doux'.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Transposition / stylization of experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Fiction must transform (transpose, stylize) raw experience rather than literally reproduce it; the novelist works in the very material out of which the object is made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because language is also the medium of thought, the writer must consciously order and stylize experience to make it art. Mere verbatim imitation of life confuses model and artist and fails aesthetically. Aim for deliberate shaping rather than photographic reproduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization as human particularity
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters should be breathing, recognizable human beings, individualized rather than schematic types.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: View each character as a product of particular material and social conditions (house, profession, inherited habits, ambitions). Draw dramatic action from characters' relations to environment as well as to each other. (Models cited: Balzac, Stendhal; anti-pattern: flat conventional puppets like stock heroes/heroines.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Match subject to talent
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose subjects that fit the novelist's power of extracting what the subject contains; know one's limits and renounce larger fields if necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An innate tendency to see in large masses may not match technical ability to render them; better to 'narrow one's vision to one's pencil' and do a small thing closely and deeply than a big thing loosely. Of many tempting subjects, only a few will be 'fit for the hand' of the writer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject must yield moral/significant response
rubrics_metrics.description: A good subject must respond in some way to the reader's unconscious question: 'What judgment on life does it contain for me?'; it should shed light on moral experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the subject cannot be expanded to illuminate moral or human experience it remains a meaningless scrap of fact. Exceptions exist only in pathological or clearly abnormal worlds that intentionally sever normal rhythms. (Anti-pattern: stories that signify nothing because they fail to provide a rational response.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality is new vision, not novel manner
rubrics_metrics.description: True originality consists not in a new manner but in a new, personal vision attained by long brooding and accumulated knowledge and experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not mistake novelty of surface technique for creative originality. Long meditation, study of the past, and a wide accumulation of impressions nourish the personal vision. (Anti-pattern: fear of imitation leading to rash novelty.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmony between talent and argument
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure a harmony between the author's talent and the argument (theme) chosen; form and style should 'spring naturally' from the theme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An author's form and style should be proportioned to his individual powers. Forcing an argument beyond one's expressive capacity produces imbalance (remedy: choose a narrower field or different subject).

rubrics_metrics.name: Double-sided creative imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: The creative imagination must be two-sided: able to penetrate into other minds and stand sufficiently aloof to relate them to the whole of life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This balance prevents confusing emotivity with its objective rendering; one must both sympathetically identify with characters and detach enough to see larger relations and meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of stream of consciousness and 'slice of life' effects — only when serving design
rubrics_metrics.description: The stream of consciousness and slice-of-life methods can be valuable but only when they serve the general design; not as ends in themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These techniques are effective for portraying a mind under acute mental stress or for specific psychological effects; greatest novelists use them sparingly where they fit the whole picture. (Anti-pattern: treating unconscious abundance as the subject itself; mere 'automatic' record of half-aware impressions.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Disengage crucial moments from the welter of existence
rubrics_metrics.description: Fiction's art is the disengaging of crucial moments from the welter of existence; choose moments that are crucial because they relate to familiar social or moral standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crucial moments need not be external events but must be recognizable as having moral or social significance that fixes attention and memory. Drama arises from conflicts between social order and individual appetites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid formlessness and equate chaos with falsity
rubrics_metrics.description: Formlessness is not a virtue; confusing chaotic emotivity with proper artistic rendering is an error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An audience's praise of 'truthful' chaos is misguided if the author cannot apprehend or define chaos artistically. Discipline and coherent shaping remain necessary to make chaos meaningful in art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not write for immediate readers/editors; write for your inner correspondent
rubrics_metrics.description: Cease thinking of readers, editors, and publishers; write for the 'other self' with whom the artist is in mysterious correspondence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focusing on immediate market or reader tastes encourages speed and shortcuts. Best work comes from attention to the inner creative impulse and long brooding on the subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style as discipline; carve trifles; revise for harmony
rubrics_metrics.description: Style is the most personal ingredient and must be disciplined; be unwilling to publish anything that is not harmoniously expressed in language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Habit and repeated refusal to accept approximate phrasing lead to a stronger style. Practice 'precious carving of trifles' — careful revision — to develop lasting style; otherwise one sets boundaries to talent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short story: give reader immediate sense of security (narrative trust)
rubrics_metrics.description: In a short story every phrase should be a sign-post and never (unless intentional) a misleading one; gain the reader's confidence so he may be led into incredible adventures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reader trust permits suspension of disbelief. The least irrelevance or inattention will break the spell. (Guideline: make narrative markers clear and consistent so readers can rely on them.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Handle improbability and the supernatural by maintaining naturalness
rubrics_metrics.description: Improbability is not in itself dangerous; the appearance of improbability is — maintain an air of naturalness and the author's sureness of foot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Especially in supernatural or ghost stories, the approach must be studied and the atmosphere perfectly maintained. The more improbable the event, the more rigorously natural the narrative voice and details must be. (Example: Turn of the Screw; anti-pattern: careless, unconvinced description.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid splintering the reader's attention; favor focused, cumulative effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not multiply horrors or elements in a way that disperses attention; if multiplied they should be cumulative and quiet iteration often works better than variety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simplification and repetition (quiet iteration) often create stronger tension than diversified assaults. Fewer, cumulative elements maintain focus and heighten effect (example: Emperor Jones).

rubrics_metrics.name: Test subjects for depth; beware the false good-subject
rubrics_metrics.description: A novelist must discern between subjects trivial in appearance and subjects trivial to the core; test whether a subject yields depth before beginning to tell it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Probe a subject mentally to see if it contains a germ that expands to moral or human significance. Mistakes in subject choice are learned against by prolonged experience; false attractions should be resisted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slow brooding and accumulated experience as necessary preparation
rubrics_metrics.description: Subjects should be long carried in the mind, brooded upon, and fed with impressions and emotions to produce a personal vision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inspiration alone is insufficient; long meditation, study of predecessors, and accumulation of knowledge deepen and personalize the vision. One strong emotional experience can supply many creations provided the artist can brood on it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose scale appropriately; prefer intimate mastery to loose grandeur
rubrics_metrics.description: If your expressive powers are limited, abandon the larger for the smaller field and do the small thing closely and deeply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many failures stem from a mismatch between the scale of vision and the capacity to render it. Better to execute a narrowly focused subject with depth than attempt sweeping panoramas inadequately handled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain moral sensibility in portrayal
rubrics_metrics.description: A novelist must retain the capacity to perceive moral qualities (including vileness) in characters; failure to see moral shadows flattens and weakens characterization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rendering vice or meanness 'in the round' increases a work's value, but unconsciously failing to perceive the ugliness of actions causes characters to lose probableness and vitality. Vigilance of moral perception is part of craft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance breadth and microscopic detail (saturation without confusion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine broad sweep of vision with exquisite delicacy of touch; saturate the subject and keep hands on main threads so no incident contributing to design escapes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use anticipatory flashes and tiny 'blazes' as sign-posts within a luxuriant narration. Mastery requires both the ability to range widely and to attend microcosmically to small human details (Proust model).
